key_insight: The paper argues that AI development must adopt a strong sustainability paradigm — one that respects absolute ecological limits (energy, materials, and ecosystems) — rather than relying on efficiency or substitution alone, requiring systemic design, governance and demand-reduction measures.
problem_solved: It addresses the lack of a rigorous sustainability framework for AI that accounts for absolute planetary limits and the AI sector’s growing material and energy footprint, preventing piecemeal solutions that delay or worsen ecological harm.
method: Define a 'strong sustainability' stance for AI that treats natural capital as non-substitutable and specifies safe operating boundaries for energy, materials and emissions.

Translate the stance into practical criteria and metrics (lifecycle footprints, material flows, absolute caps) and propose design principles (frugality, reuse, durability) for models and infrastructure.
Recommend governance levers and policy tools (sectoral caps, procurement rules, disclosure standards) to align AI R&D and deployment with planetary limits.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this reframes optimization goals from mere efficiency to compliance with absolute environmental limits, pushing teams to prioritize low-footprint model design, transparent lifecycle accounting, and demand-side interventions.
visual_elements: Side-by-side comparison: 'Weak vs Strong Sustainability' with icons and short policy/design implications
Lifecycle Sankey chart of AI model impacts (manufacturing, training, inference, data centers, e-waste) with hotspots highlighted
Compact checklist/flowchart of actionable design principles (frugal architectures, benchmarking, reuse, disclosure) linked to governance levers
Bar or area chart mapping proposed sectoral caps against current/forecasted AI resource use to show the gap
paper_title: A strong sustainability approach to AI development
